❓ My question
What can a fourteen-year-old narrator show you that a grown-up might miss?
Try it
The narrator uses I and me to tell the story from inside the events.
A first-person narrator can tell us exactly what every other character is thinking.
The reader can only know what the narrator notices, remembers, or chooses to share.
Make a first guess. What can a teenage narrator show you?

🗞️ Where Are We?
EVENING EDITION · 1965

Ponyboy’s world has Corvairs and Mustangs, a movie house, and a movie star he wishes he looked like. Tap the street that is his.

  1. Born in Tulsa
    S. E. Hinton was born in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
  2. 1967
    The Outsiders, her first novel, was published by Viking.
  3. A teenage writer
    She was still a teenager when the book came out.
  4. Somewhere in the Southwest
    The book never names its city. Ponyboy says only that he lives in the Southwest (Hinton, Ch. 1).
Sources: S. E. Hinton’s official site (sehinton.com); Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture. Street scenes drawn for this lesson.

✏️ Daily Oral Language
✅ Correct model
Soda and Steve worked at the same gas station; Soda worked full time.
1 names take capitals2 same time all through3 two whole thoughts, joined

Use the model to fix the sentence below.

🔧 Fix this one
ponyboy walks home from the movie house alone, he wished he had some company
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

Ponyboy walked home from the movie house alone; he wished he had some company. The name Ponyboy takes a capital. The first verb slid into the present (walks) while the second stayed in the past (wished), so both go in the past: walked, wished. The sentence holds two complete thoughts, and a comma alone cannot join them. A semicolon works, and so does a period with a capital He.

🔤 Words: Chapter 1

Say the meaning first, then tap the card to check.

⚡
reckless
tap to flip and hear it
reckless
Not caring about danger; wild and careless. “a finely drawn, sensitive face that somehow manages to be reckless and thoughtful at the same time” (Hinton, Ch. 1)
🌊
unfathomable
tap to flip and hear it
unfathomable
Impossible to understand or explain. “He liked fights, blondes, and for some unfathomable reason, school.” (Hinton, Ch. 1)
🧐
sagely
tap to flip and hear it
sagely
Wisely, like someone who knows. Here, joking. “Two-Bit nodded sagely.” (Hinton, Ch. 1) Two-Bit is joking: he acts like an expert on looking tough.
💎
rarities
tap to flip and hear it
rarities
Things that seldom happen or are seldom found. “organized gangs are rarities” (Hinton, Ch. 1)
🙄
sarcasm
tap to flip and hear it
sarcasm
Saying the opposite of what you mean, to mock or sting. “trying for Soda’s sake to keep the sarcasm out of my voice” (Hinton, Ch. 1) Ponyboy says Sure, but means the opposite.

Professor Lovelore

Here is what to hold onto. Everything in this book comes through one boy who says I. That is first-person point of view. You get his eyes, his feelings, his words. You also get his mistakes. Ponyboy tells you he doesn’t care about Darry, and then admits he is lying. A careful reader listens to the narrator, and checks him too.

You have read, and you have listened to the narrator. Now open his sketchbook.

Part 1Chapter ThinkingComplete sentences, with details from the text.
1. How does Ponyboy describe the difference between greasers and Socs? What do his word choices show about how he feels about it? Use one detail. Cite like this: (Hinton, Ch. 1).
2. Darry and Soda both love Ponyboy, but they show it differently. What does each one do in Chapter 1 that shows it?
3. The chapter ends with Ponyboy saying he lies to himself all the time. How does that change the way you read everything he told you before it?
Part 2Quick Write 1: From the InsideStep 1 of 3: plan
1 Plan2 Draft3 Revise
From the Inside. Think of two groups of people who are divided from each other by background, neighborhood, interest, reputation, or something similar. They can come from your own life, from history, from another book, or from your imagination. Describe what it is like to belong to one of those groups, from the inside: what does belonging feel like? What do you notice, value, or fear that someone outside the group might not see?
